title: Review: Energy levels and spectra; Nuclear structure and notation; Rutherford scattering and atomic models; Bohr model of hydrogen
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Physics 2 (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: Q02-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; Q06-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; Q04-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; Q04-1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: N01-1#N.10, Q02-1#N.13b, Q04-1#N.10b, Q06-1#N.14b, N01-1#N.7b, Q04-1#N.8b, Q06-1#N.7b, N01-1#N.3, Q04-1#N.11b, N01-1#N.5. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Emission line spectrum
items.clue: Bright features on a dark background, produced by a hot gas at low pressure.

items.label: Atom
items.clue: About 10⁻¹⁰ m across: roughly 10⁴ to 10⁵ times wider than its positive core.

items.label: Bohr model
items.clue: 1913 picture of hydrogen: one electron on allowed circular orbits around one proton.

items.label: Ground state
items.clue: The n = 1 orbit of hydrogen, with radius 5.29 × 10⁻¹¹ m and exactly one λ around it.

questions.stem: Which pair are isotopes of the same element?

options.text: ⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴⁰₁₉K
³¹₁₅P and ³²₁₆S
²³₁₁Na and ²³₁₁Na⁺
³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl

questions.stem: The energy levels of a hypothetical single-electron atom are −6.0 eV, −5.5 eV, −2.0 eV, and −1.0 eV, and the atom is ionized when its energy reaches 0 eV. An atom in its ground state is struck by a photon of energy 4.5 eV. What happens?

options.text: The atom absorbs 4.0 eV, and a photon of energy 0.5 eV continues on.
The photon is not absorbed, and it continues on with energy 4.5 eV.
The photon is absorbed, and the atom's energy becomes −1.5 eV.
The photon is absorbed, and the atom ends in the −1.0 eV level.

questions.stem: Predict first. Which statement correctly describes the Bohr model of the atom?

options.text: The accepted present-day picture of the atom, in which the electrons really move in circles
A model in which gravity between the electron and the nucleus sets the size of each orbit
A classical model in which the electron can orbit at any radius and so can have any energy
An early model that used classical force and motion and led to discrete energy states for hydrogen

questions.stem: A museum model of a hydrogen atom shows the nucleus as a ball 1 cm across, with the atom built to the same scale. About how wide must the model atom be?

options.text: About 2 cm, as the nucleus takes up most of the atom
About 10 m, as the atom is about a thousand times as wide
Between about 100 m and 1 km
More than 1000 km, as the atom is about 10⁸ times as wide

questions.explanation: The atom is about 10⁴ to 10⁵ times as wide as its nucleus: 1 cm × 10⁴ = 100 m, 1 cm × 10⁵ = 1 km. A hydrogen atom is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m across and its nucleus (one proton) about 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m, so about 600 m.

questions.stem: Predict first. Two protons are held 1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m apart, a typical separation of nucleons in a nucleus. They are then moved apart until they are 1 × 10⁻¹³ m apart, 100 times farther. How does the strong force between them at the larger separation compare with the strong force at the smaller separation?

options.text: It is smaller by a factor of 10⁴, the same factor by which the electric repulsion falls
It is negligible, far smaller than their electric repulsion at the larger separation
It is equal, since the strong force does not depend on how far apart they are
It is larger, as the pull of a rubber band grows when the band is stretched

questions.stem: In the standing-wave model of the hydrogen atom, the electron's orbit in the n = 2 state has 4 times the radius of its orbit in the n = 1 state. What is the ratio λ₂/λ₁ of the electron's de Broglie wavelength in the n = 2 state to its de Broglie wavelength in the n = 1 state?

Predict first. A student claims that most of the mass of an atom is outside its nucleus, because the electrons occupy nearly all of the atom's volume. Which response to the student's claim is correct?

options.text: The claim is wrong: a proton or a neutron has nearly two thousand times an electron's mass.
The claim is wrong: electrons and nucleons have similar masses, so the mass is shared evenly.
The claim is right: the part of the atom that fills nearly all its volume has most of the mass.
The claim is wrong: the nucleus fills most of the atom's volume, so most of the mass is in it.

questions.stem: A nucleus of potassium-40 is written in nuclear notation as ⁴⁰₁₉K. Which statement about this nucleus is correct?

options.text: It contains 40 neutrons.
It contains 19 neutrons.
It contains 19 nucleons.
It contains 21 neutrons.

questions.stem: In the standing-wave model of the hydrogen atom, the electron in the n = 3 state moves in a circular orbit of radius 4.77 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. What is the speed of the electron? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
Predict first. Carbon-12 (¹²₆C) and carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C) are isotopes of carbon. Which statement about these two nuclides is correct?

options.text: They contain the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons.
Both contain the same number of protons, but different numbers of neutrons.
Their atoms have different chemical properties, as their nuclei differ.
Their nuclei are identical, but their atoms have different numbers of electrons.
